paragraphs.text: Later on, the Bengali intonation was recognized as a Gaoŕiiya style of intonation. At Allahabad (Prayag) there was an assembly of the Brahmins of Jambudviipa (India) about 1200 or 1300 years ago, in which they declared that the culture of Bengal was different from that of other areas. It was a blended civilization, a blending of Ráŕhii and Mongolian civilizations. It could not be accepted as a Vedic culture. So ten categories of Brahmins were recognized as the bonafide Brahmins of India. Regarding the other Brahmins it was declared that they were non-Brahmins using Brahmin surnames. The ten recognized categories of Brahmins were: 1) the Sárasvata Brahmins of Punjab and Kashmir, 2) the Gaoŕa Brahmins of Rajasthan, 3) the Kányakubja Brahmins of Uttar Pradesh, 4) the Maethil Brahmins of Mithila of Bihar, 5) the Nágara Brahmins of Gujarat. These five categories were declared Paiṋcagaoŕii, that is, the five recognized groups of northern India. And the five recognized categories of Brahmins of southern India, known as Paiṋcadrávid́ii, were: 1) the Citpávana Brahmins of Maharastra, 2) the Utkala Brahmins of Odisha, 3) the Kannad́a Brahmins of Karnataka, 4) the Támil Brahmins of Chennai [Tamil Nadu] and 5) the Traelauṋga Brahmins of Andhra Pradesh. Those are the only recognized classes of Brahmins of India. The remaining – Ráŕhii, Bárendra, Dakśinátya Vaedika, Páshcáttya Vaedika – are not recognized Brahmins but rather have been declared as non-Brahmins using Brahmin surnames.
summary: Later on, the Bengali intonation was recognized as a Gaoŕiiya style of intonation.
Regarding the other Brahmins it was declared that they were non-Brahmins using Brahmin surnames.
The remaining – Ráŕhii, Bárendra, Dakśinátya Vaedika, Páshcáttya Vaedika – are not recognized Brahmins but rather have been declared as non-Brahmins using Brahmin surnames.

paragraphs.text: The Mongolian civilization that flourished in the Brahmaputra Valley blended with the Ráŕhii civilization and the Gangetic civilization, resulting in a new blended civilization, the Gaoŕiiya or Bengal civilization. Tantra had its origin in such a blended civilization. The Ganges and the Brahmaputra meet at Goyalanda in Bengal. Thus we see that the Bengalee civilization is a mixed civilization, a blending of the Gondwana civilization of Ráŕh, the Gangetic civilization of northern India, and the Mongolian civilization of Tibet and China [whose access was via the Brahmaputra Valley]. That is why it is said that Bengalee civilization flourished in the border areas between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa.
summary: The Mongolian civilization that flourished in the Brahmaputra Valley blended with the Ráŕhii civilization and the Gangetic civilization, resulting in a new blended civilization, the Gaoŕiiya or Bengal civilization.
The Ganges and the Brahmaputra meet at Goyalanda in Bengal.
That is why it is said that Bengalee civilization flourished in the border areas between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa.

paragraphs.text: In the Bengalee race the blood of these different civilizations is mixed. Due to the Australoid and Dravidoid blood of Ráŕh, the people of Bankura, Midnapore and Purulia are mostly dark-complexioned. A certain amount of Mongolian blood is also present. The Bengalee farmers, the Rajbangshis and Chakmas, have come from the Brahmaputra Valley. They are flat-nosed. As a result of the permutation and combination of these various small groups, the various castes and sub-castes of West Bengal emerged – the Brahmins, Kayasthas, Vaidyas, and a host of sub-castes. However, the source of all these castes and sub-castes is one and the same – the blended culture of the Ráŕh, Gangetic and Brahmaputra valleys. If we take Bengal as a distinct land, it has a speciality of its own. This is due to the influence of the river valleys.
summary: In the Bengalee race the blood of these different civilizations is mixed.
As a result of the permutation and combination of these various small groups, the various castes and sub-castes of West Bengal emerged – the Brahmins, Kayasthas, Vaidyas, and a host of sub-castes.
This is due to the influence of the river valleys.

paragraphs.text: The geographical environment hugely influences human expressions. Consequently, different schools of music and dance arose in various parts of Bengal. The same thing is taking place even today and will do so in the future as well. The topography which has resulted from the meeting of the three rivers has exerted a great influence on the Bengalee mentality. By temperament the Bengalees are a sentimental people. Sometimes they tolerate injustice for a long period without any murmur, without even a whimper. Suddenly they decide not to tolerate injustice any longer, and they rise in revolt. In a few days they become involved in a bloody rebellion. Although prior to that they were subjected to endless torture, insult and humiliation, they tolerated all the wrongs and injustices like a nation of lifeless corpses. These are the signs of a sentimental race. The people of Bengal, particularly the people of the lower stratum of society, had to undergo tremendous torture and humiliation in the past. Suddenly they revolted and embraced Islam in large numbers. That group are also Bengalees – in bone, flesh and blood. They became Muslims as a reaction to the exploitation by the contemporary society.
summary: The geographical environment hugely influences human expressions.
In a few days they become involved in a bloody rebellion.
They became Muslims as a reaction to the exploitation by the contemporary society.

paragraphs.text: (The Jains of Bengal, particularly those of Bankura, Midnapur and Purulia, discarded the Jain religion and accepted the Vaeśńava religion [Vaishnavism] of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in large numbers. Even today the Jain temples exist, but there are no Jain worshippers.)
summary: (The Jains of Bengal, particularly those of Bankura, Midnapur and Purulia, discarded the Jain religion and accepted the Vaeśńava religion [Vaishnavism] of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in large numbers.
Even today the Jain temples exist, but there are no Jain worshippers.

paragraphs.text: This sentimentality is one of the specialities of the Bengalee character. The Bengalees, by struggling against the original culture of ancient Gondwanaland, the original cultural trend of the Gangetic Valley and also the pure Mongolian culture of the Brahmaputra Valley, have built a new, integrated Bengalee culture of their own. This typical Bengalee culture emerged about three thousand years ago. That is, about 3500 years ago the Bengali language had its very old structure. That old structure of the Bengali language, through evolutionary changes, has taken the form of the modern Bengali language. Modern Bengali is about eight hundred to one thousand years old. Thus, after the Bengalees distinguished themselves in so many ways, they thought that the ups and downs of their social life also should be regulated in a particular flow, which is neither wholly in conformity with the full-fledged matriarchal system of Gondwanaland, nor the full-fledged patriarchal system of the Gangetic Valley, nor the Mongolian, female-dominated system of the Brahmaputra Valley.
summary: This sentimentality is one of the specialities of the Bengalee character.
That is, about 3500 years ago the Bengali language had its very old structure.

Thus, after the Bengalees distinguished themselves in so many ways, they thought that the ups and downs of their social life also should be regulated in a particular flow, which is neither wholly in conformity with the full-fledged matriarchal system of Gondwanaland, nor the full-fledged patriarchal system of the Gangetic Valley, nor the Mongolian, female-dominated system of the Brahmaputra Valley.

paragraphs.text: In the ancient social system of Bengal, the women had a preponderant role. Members of that society would introduce themselves by the name of their mothers. As a rule, to find out the identity of a person, people would ask a person, “Whatʼs your name? Whatʼs your motherʼs name? Whatʼs your grandmotherʼs name?”. Among the Khashiyas of Meghalaya, this system is still in vogue. Bengal has long discarded the system, because it was not conducive to the growth of the Bengalees. The Bengalees built a diverse social system which contained certain characteristics of both the matriarchal and patriarchal societies, according to necessity.
summary: In the ancient social system of Bengal, the women had a preponderant role.
Whatʼs your grandmotherʼs name?
The Bengalees built a diverse social system which contained certain characteristics of both the matriarchal and patriarchal societies, according to necessity.

paragraphs.text: For instance, in the rest of India, the property of the maternal uncle, if he dies without an heir, goes to the relatives of the father. The property of Mr. Shukla will be inherited by his cousins or their descendants, though they might be his distant relations: Mr. Shuklaʼs own sistersʼ sons will not be entitled to the property. But Bengalʼs social system is different. If a maternal uncle dies without any heir, his property will be inherited by his sistersʼ sons and not the more distant relations. This is the law of inheritance of Bengal, which is quite different from that of the rest of India. In the rest of India, property is not inherited by members of different lineages. If the maternal uncleʼs property goes to the sisterʼs son, it means it goes to a different lineage. If the maternal uncle is one Mr. Banerjee, and the sisterʼs son is a Mr. Chatterjee, and Mr. Banerjee belongs to Sáńd́ilya lineage and Mr. Chatterjee to Káshyapa lineage, the property of the Sáńd́ilyas cannot be inherited by the Káshyapas. So it is seen that the property of the maternal uncle in northern India does not go to other lineages, but it happens in Bengal.
summary: For instance, in the rest of India, the property of the maternal uncle, if he dies without an heir, goes to the relatives of the father.
In the rest of India, property is not inherited by members of different lineages.
So it is seen that the property of the maternal uncle in northern India does not go to other lineages, but it happens in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: There is yet another speciality of the Bengalee social system. In the rest of India, a daughter, after marriage, loses the identity of her fatherʼs family. But in Bengal this is not the case. According to the pandits of Bengal, a girl, after marriage, becomes a member of a new lineage no doubt. Suppose a girl of the Bose family marries into the Mitra family, it is true that her surname changes from Bose to Mitra but she still keeps her old blood; this fact cannot be ignored. She may marry into the Mitra family but she still carries the blood of the Bose family. That is why a system was introduced whereby a girl, even after marriage, will have to observe ashaoca [a purificatory period of mourning] for at least three nights after the death of any of her parentʼs family. However, in the rest of India this period of mourning is not required for a married woman because now she is the member of a different lineage. Bengal adopted a system of its own because its culture is not the unmixed Gangetic culture, but a blended culture of Gangetic, Ráŕhii and Brahmaputra Valley cultures.
summary: There is yet another speciality of the Bengalee social system.
Suppose a girl of the Bose family marries into the Mitra family, it is true that her surname changes from Bose to Mitra but she still keeps her old blood; this fact cannot be ignored.
Bengal adopted a system of its own because its culture is not the unmixed Gangetic culture, but a blended culture of Gangetic, Ráŕhii and Brahmaputra Valley cultures.

paragraphs.text: So wealth remains on the maternal uncleʼs side; and also if anyone dies on that side, three daysʼ ashaoca is observed; such practicalities are observed. This is how the practicalities of life have been accepted in the social system.
summary: So wealth remains on the maternal uncleʼs side; and also if anyone dies on that side, three daysʼ ashaoca is observed; such practicalities are observed.
This is how the practicalities of life have been accepted in the social system.

paragraphs.text: Next comes the question of the law of inheritance. The rest of India is governed by the Mitákśará law of inheritance, which is based on the Manu Saḿhitá(4) [as interpreted] by Vyasadeva. Bengal is governed by the Dáyabhága system,(5) which is based on the interpretation of the Manu Saḿhitá by Jiimutabahana. In northern India, sons are entitled to ancestral property even during the lifetime of their fathers. In fact, the children, even when they are in their mothersʼ wombs, acquire the right to property. When they are grown up, they can obtain their share by filing lawsuits against their fathers. But this is not permissible in the Dáyabhága laws of Bengal. As long as the fathers are alive, only they can inherit ancestral property, and they remain the sole owners of any inherited ancestral property. And if a father so likes, he can deprive his sons of their ancestral property: he may disown his son, or he may transfer the property right to other persons outside his own family. In the rest of India, there is no law to disown oneʼs son. Only Bengal follows that system, the Dáyabhága system of inheritance.
summary: Next comes the question of the law of inheritance.
When they are grown up, they can obtain their share by filing lawsuits against their fathers.
Only Bengal follows that system, the Dáyabhága system of inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Not only this, there is proof that girls have a particular type of legal relationship with their parents in Bengal. One hundred years ago there was a rule. Suppose a girlʼs name is Maya and she was born into the Basu family and married into the Mitra family. How will she maintain a relationship with her parents? Before marriage she writes her name as Maya Basu Duhitá [duhitá means “daughter”], whereas after marriage she writes her name as Maya Mitra Jáyá [jáyá means “wife”]. Even after marriage, if she so wished she could write her name as Maya Basu Duhitá. After all, she was a daughter of the Basu family. This proves the fact that even after a girlʼs marriage, her relationship with her parents is not permanently severed. This tradition has continued in Bengal.
summary: Not only this, there is proof that girls have a particular type of legal relationship with their parents in Bengal.
Before marriage she writes her name as Maya Basu Duhitá [duhitá means “daughter”], whereas after marriage she writes her name as Maya Mitra Jáyá [jáyá means “wife”].
This tradition has continued in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: Bengalee culture and civilization emerged [particularly] from its own soil, whereas the culture and civilization of the rest of India is a product of its environment [in general]. There is some difference between the two. Bengalee civilization is indigenous, as Bengal is predominantly a land of water. People have to remain constantly vigilant as to whether there is solid ground under their feet or not. There are some places in East Bengal where the land remains under water for seven months during the year. As long as there is sufficient water in lakes and rivers, the girls can easily go to see their parents. But the rest of the year they cannot, as there is no land route. Boats can ply only when there is water. There are no bullock-carts. So if water recedes, how can they move?
summary: Bengalee culture and civilization emerged [particularly] from its own soil, whereas the culture and civilization of the rest of India is a product of its environment [in general].
As long as there is sufficient water in lakes and rivers, the girls can easily go to see their parents.
So if water recedes, how can they move?

paragraphs.text: Now let us consider the influence of kings on the social system. In the rest of India, kings came to power through hereditary rights. However, in the history of Bengal, in a number of cases, the situation was different. You should remember that ninety-nine percent of Bengalees are the indigenous population – they are the children of the soil. There are only a few communities who are the original Bengalees, the forefathers of the Bengalee race: the remaining castes and sub-castes have descended from them. Those who are regarded as the so-called upper castes – like delicacies placed on top of a pile of offerings – are also born of these original Bengalees. The original Bengalees are the 1) Kaevartta, 2) Mahato, 3) Gop [Sadgop], 4) Namashudra, 5) Rajbangshi and 6) Chakma. The Chakmas are original Bengalees. Today, unfortunately, the same Chakmas are treated as tribal people of the hills. These six communities comprised the original Bengalees. Due to the intermixture of these different groups, the so-called upper castes evolved, and they later became social parasites. These six ethnic groups are the pillars of Bengalee society: they support the Bengalee social structure. They can be likened to the lamp stand, whereas the so-called upper castes are the lamp, sitting on the ethnic Bengalees. The oil trickling down falls on their bodies. When only the five categories of Gaoŕiiya Brahmins and the five categories of Dravidian Brahmins were recognized – not only the Brahmins of Bengal but also the other upper castes of Bengal were unrecognized – it was decided according to the Raghunandan social system of Bengal that the Brahmins who were not recognized by northern India, declared to be outcastes, would be treated as the Brahmins of Bengal, because they were the persons who had to conduct the religious worship. The remaining non-Brahmins were declared as Shúdras.
summary: Now let us consider the influence of kings on the social system.
Today, unfortunately, the same Chakmas are treated as tribal people of the hills.
The remaining non-Brahmins were declared as Shúdras.

paragraphs.text: The Vedic system is that of caturvarńa [four classes, racial-caste order] in the society [Vaeshya, Vipra, Kśatriya and Shúdra]. But in Bengal there were only two classes – Vipra and Shúdra. Kśatriyas and Vaeshyas were conspicuously lacking in the society of Bengal.
summary: The Vedic system is that of caturvarńa [four classes, racial-caste order] in the society [Vaeshya, Vipra, Kśatriya and Shúdra].
But in Bengal there were only two classes – Vipra and Shúdra.
Kśatriyas and Vaeshyas were conspicuously lacking in the society of Bengal.

paragraphs.text: In the rest of India one of the main sources of livelihood for the Brahmins was the practice of ayurveda. However, since the Brahmins of Bengal were not recognized by North India, those Brahmins who continued the practice of ayurveda in Bengal were also unrecognized. They were considered as a separate caste, Vaidya, whereas in fact they are also Brahmins. So, since there is a difference from the scriptural point of view, there is also a difference regarding the system of worship.
summary: In the rest of India one of the main sources of livelihood for the Brahmins was the practice of ayurveda.
They were considered as a separate caste, Vaidya, whereas in fact they are also Brahmins.
So, since there is a difference from the scriptural point of view, there is also a difference regarding the system of worship.

paragraphs.text: Kings ascended the throne through the hereditary system in northern India. Only recently in India, a certain queen wanted to install her son as king. This is possible in northern India but not in Bengal. In Bengal the monarchy was not a hereditary institution. That is, whenever a king was found to be not properly discharging his royal duties, then those six ethnic Bengalee communities would revolt against him. The Kaevarttas of Midnapur created tremendous problems for the kings of Orissa and the nawabs of Bengal, and Kaevarttas of central Bengal organized a rebellion during the reign of Devapal II during the Buddhist period. That is why when the kings of Bengal installed their heirs on the throne as crown princes, they requested their subjects to extend support to their (the kingsʼ) decision. The kings of northern India, however, when installing their princely heirs on the throne, used to tell their subjects, “Accept them as the new kings obey this directive”. The one was a request, the other an order.
summary: Kings ascended the throne through the hereditary system in northern India.
That is, whenever a king was found to be not properly discharging his royal duties, then those six ethnic Bengalee communities would revolt against him.
The one was a request, the other an order.

paragraphs.text: This is how the social system of Bengal evolved, as a result of which many dissimilarities [with other parts of India] became noticeable during the historical battles.
summary: This is how the social system of Bengal evolved, as a result of which many dissimilarities [with other parts of India] became noticeable during the historical battles.

paragraphs.text: During the war between the Kaoravas and the Pandavas, the kings of Bengal did not take part. “The war will do no good to Bengal,” they thought, and hence they did not want to engage themselves in unnecessary spilling of blood. “Why should thousands of soldiers die for nothing?” they argued. So they remained neutral. Due to this psychology, the kings of Bengal have always fought against the emperors of Delhi, from the Hindu era through the Mughal and Pathan eras. They have always waged war against Delhi. There has been a constant ideological conflict between Delhi and Bengal.
summary: During the war between the Kaoravas and the Pandavas, the kings of Bengal did not take part.
So they remained neutral.
There has been a constant ideological conflict between Delhi and Bengal.

paragraphs.text: An interesting observation about North India is that the year is calculated according to the lunar calendar. It was supposed that the earth is stationary and the moon revolves around it. Of course, in actual fact the earth is not stationary but revolves around the sun. The moon also rotates, and it takes anywhere from twenty-eight to thirty-one days for the moon to complete one rotation (lunar month). If we multiply the lunar month by twelve we get a lunar year of 354 or 355 days. In northern India this system of calculation is prevalent. The eleventh or twelfth day of the fortnight is determined according to the zodiac sign and the lunar days. In northern India ekádashii means the eleventh day of the month and dvádashii means the twelfth day of the month and trayodashii means the thirteenth day. On the eleventh day, if there is tryáhasparsha – that is, if there is a meeting of three tithis or lunar days in one twenty-four-hour span – then the eleventh day will be followed by the thirteenth day in North India. So the dvádashii or twelfth day will not occur. Obviously there are many disadvantages in this calculation. You might have noticed on many occasions during the Durga Puja festival, the seventh day (Saptamii) is followed by the ninth day (Navamii). It happens due to this very reason. This is highly disadvantageous because people will not be able to utilize the intervening day. The astrologers of Bengal pondered deeply on this problem.
summary: An interesting observation about North India is that the year is calculated according to the lunar calendar.
In northern India ekádashii means the eleventh day of the month and dvádashii means the twelfth day of the month and trayodashii means the thirteenth day.
The astrologers of Bengal pondered deeply on this problem.

paragraphs.text: The viḿshottariiya system of astrological calculation, followed by the Varanasi astrologers, is different from that of the calculations of the astrologers of Bengal. Here there is not much scope to discuss astrology in detail. Let me explain concisely. Let us suppose that if a person lives an average of 120 years, and if the calculation is made accordingly, the system is called viḿshottariiya, and if a person lives for an average of 108 years, the system is called aśt́ottariiya.
summary: The viḿshottariiya system of astrological calculation, followed by the Varanasi astrologers, is different from that of the calculations of the astrologers of Bengal.
Let me explain concisely.

Let us suppose that if a person lives an average of 120 years, and if the calculation is made accordingly, the system is called viḿshottariiya, and if a person lives for an average of 108 years, the system is called aśt́ottariiya.

paragraphs.text: Now the question is, whether human beings can survive for 120 years or not: usually they do not. However that may be, the systems of calculation are different. The authorities of ayurveda in northern India act according to the ayurveda of the Vedas, and the Vaidyas [physicians] of Bengal follow the vaedyaka shástra [Tantric system of medicine given by Lord Shiva]. There is a vast difference between the two. In vaedyaka shástra there is a provision for the dissection of dead bodies; but in northern India, there is no such permission. Anyone doing so will risk becoming an outcaste. And so there is a standing rule in northern India that the Vaidyas of Bengal are not recognized as Brahmins, although according to the liberal social system of Bengal, the Vaidyas should be recognized as Brahmins. I do not believe in casteism; I am just trying to point out the facts.
summary: Now the question is, whether human beings can survive for 120 years or not: usually they do not.
In vaedyaka shástra there is a provision for the dissection of dead bodies; but in northern India, there is no such permission.
I do not believe in casteism; I am just trying to point out the facts.

paragraphs.text: So it is seen that the systems of astrological calculation are different in Bengal and northern India. There is a clear difference in the systems of lunar calendar and solar calendar. I will try now to explain briefly the system of the solar calendar. Let us suppose that the earth is stationary and the sun is moving around the earth. Of course the reality is different: the sun is stationary, and the earth is moving around the sun. In actuality, the sun is not stationary either. The sun, together with the planets, satellites, etc., is moving in orbit in the galaxy.
summary: So it is seen that the systems of astrological calculation are different in Bengal and northern India.
Of course the reality is different: the sun is stationary, and the earth is moving around the sun.
, is moving in orbit in the galaxy.

paragraphs.text: A father, a mother and their children sit close together in a railway compartment, talking among themselves and eating dainties and delicacies. Are they motionless or static? They are not motionless: they are also moving along with the train, and they also reach Delhi from Kolkata. In the same manner, the sun, together with the planets and satellites, is also moving, although the mutual distance between them appears to always be the same. It seems that the sun is fixed, but actually the sun is moving.
summary: A father, a mother and their children sit close together in a railway compartment, talking among themselves and eating dainties and delicacies.
They are not motionless: they are also moving along with the train, and they also reach Delhi from Kolkata.
It seems that the sun is fixed, but actually the sun is moving.

paragraphs.text: Now, if the earth is taken to be fixed, the sun takes about 365 or 366 days to complete one round of movement around the earth: this is one solar year. In the case of the moon, there is the month first, and if those months are multiplied by twelve, this is the lunar year. In the case of the sun, first there is the year. By dividing the number of days in the year by twelve, we get the months. How do we divide? The void containing the sun and the moon is a 360 degree void. In this path of movement lie the different stellar constellations, each one of which resembles a certain figure. There is one constellation that looks like a sheep. So it is named Meśa [Aries]. Another looks like a bull. So it is called Vrśa [Taurus]. Thus we get the twelve signs of the zodiac covering 360 degrees – Meśa, Vrśa, Mithuna, Karkat́a, Siḿhá, Kanyá, Tulá, Vrshcik, Dhanu, Makar, Kumbha and Miina. Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces are the Roman names.(6) Each one forms an angle of thirty degrees at the centre. So the twelve signs make 360 degrees. The time taken by the sun to cross a particular arc opposite the thirty-degree angle comprises one solar month. So, if we divide the year by twelve we also get one month. According to the Bengalee calendar, the first part of the arc does not enter the calculation, only the last part. The first part of an arc is added to the previous arc; this is the system of reckoning in Bengal. However, in Punjab or Kashmir the first part of the arc and not the last part is taken into the calculation. That is why yesterday [the day before the Bengalee New Yearʼs day] was New Yearʼs Day in the Punjab, because they calculate on the basis of the first part of the arc. The Bengali month thus ends one day after the Punjabi month. And what has the Punjab done? They have calculated the time according to the last part of the arc. This is the system of the solar calendar.
summary: Now, if the earth is taken to be fixed, the sun takes about 365 or 366 days to complete one round of movement around the earth: this is one solar year.
Each one forms an angle of thirty degrees at the centre.
This is the system of the solar calendar.

paragraphs.text: Regarding the solar calendar, I would like to add something more here, because there is only this similarity between North India and Bengal. Ancient Bengal rejected the North Indian system of calculating time a long time ago – about 3500 years ago. So we see that the Bengalee culture is at least 3500 years old, perhaps even older. The northern system of calculation is the lunar system, which centers around the full moons. The full moon has to take place in the moon of that particular planet. So, the moon has to move along a similar orbit.
summary: Regarding the solar calendar, I would like to add something more here, because there is only this similarity between North India and Bengal.
The northern system of calculation is the lunar system, which centers around the full moons.
So, the moon has to move along a similar orbit.

paragraphs.text: So a Bengalee month is named after the zodiac sign within which the full moon takes place. For instance, to cross the area of Aries (Meśa) the sun takes thirty-one days (this zodiac sign is not very big – there are zodiac signs which are larger, and it takes thirty-two days for the sun to cross them). The Bengalee months Áśáŕh and Shrávańa sometimes are as long as thirty-two days. Of the two calendars, Bengalee and English, the Bengalee calendar is more scientific. The Bengalee calendar mentions the exact number of days which a planet takes to cross the area of the zodiac sign concerned, but ordinary people do not realize exactly how many days it takes – thirty, thirty-one or thirty-two. So although the English calendar is unscientific, still it has one practical advantage: the number of days of each month is fixed. The sun exists in a thirty degree arc-centre for the whole Bengalee month. The full moon takes place within the constellation of Vishákhá star; so the name of the Bengalee month is Vaeshákh – son of Vishákhá, Vishákháya puttrah ityarthe. In the next month, the full moon takes place within the Jyaeśt́ha constellation; so the name of the month has become Jyaeśt́ha. However, in this regard, there is no adjustment of Kerala with North India. But in Kerala, this month of Vaeshákh [there the duration of the month is the same] is called Meśa because it is in the zodiac sign of Meśa.
summary: So a Bengalee month is named after the zodiac sign within which the full moon takes place.
So although the English calendar is unscientific, still it has one practical advantage: the number of days of each month is fixed.
But in Kerala, this month of Vaeshákh [there the duration of the month is the same] is called Meśa because it is in the zodiac sign of Meśa.

paragraphs.text: The people of Bengal noted that if 354 days make up a year according to the lunar calendar, then the year will advance by ten or twelve days in one year. The year will advance by more than one month in three years. So while people harvest in the month of Agraháyań this year, after three years the time of harvesting will fall in the Mágha month. But that is not actually the time for harvesting; so harvesting time would have to be adjusted with the months. However, if we follow the solar calendar, then sowing, harvesting, etc., will maintain adjustment with the seasons. So the lunar calendar is impractical and we should not follow it; shráddha [last rite] ceremonies, marriage ceremonies, etc., may be conducted according to the North Indian lunar calendar, for these social ceremonies must be performed within a particular auspicious period (tithi) and this cannot be determined by the solar calendar.
summary: The people of Bengal noted that if 354 days make up a year according to the lunar calendar, then the year will advance by ten or twelve days in one year.
However, if we follow the solar calendar, then sowing, harvesting, etc.

, may be conducted according to the North Indian lunar calendar, for these social ceremonies must be performed within a particular auspicious period (tithi) and this cannot be determined by the solar calendar.

paragraphs.text: Now while adjusting with the people of North India, some practical difficulties may arise. The people of northern India suggested, “All right, every three years, one month will have to be increased. But, how to adjust that extra month? One solution may be that every third year would comprise thirteen months; then there may be some sort of adjustment with North India.” Since then North India has declared that every third year consists of thirteen months. Suppose that the additional month comes after the month of Kárttik (because at that time an additional thirty days has been accumulated); the people of northern India will call it “Adhik Kártiik”. After this Adhik Kárttik comes the Agraháyań month. This additional Kárttik is called Malmás in Bengal. This is the system in Bengal.
summary: Now while adjusting with the people of North India, some practical difficulties may arise.
” Since then North India has declared that every third year consists of thirteen months.
This is the system in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: This system of astrological calculation was first introduced in Bengal by King Shalibahan of southern Bengal. Here southern Bengal means the area from the point where the Suvarnarekha [roughly on the present border between Jharkhand and West Bengal] flows into the Bay of Bengal – that is, Ramnagar Police Station, Bhograi-Kaksai, Bhograi-Baleswar – to the line from where the [Naf flows into the Bay of Bengal] up along the Chittagong-Arakan border.(7) This was the entire southern Bengal which was once part of the Sundarbans Forest. Now the Sundarbans Forest has been cleared in most districts; only about four thousand square miles is left. Out of this total area, 3400 square miles of forest are in Khulna and 600 square miles are in 24 Parganas. Formerly it was a vast forest area.
summary: This system of astrological calculation was first introduced in Bengal by King Shalibahan of southern Bengal.
Now the Sundarbans Forest has been cleared in most districts; only about four thousand square miles is left.
Formerly it was a vast forest area.

paragraphs.text: In olden days southern Bengal was known as Samatat. Later on, the Samatat area meant Murshidabad, Nadia, Jessore, Khulna, 24 Parganas and Kolkata. The area lying to the west of the Bhagirathi was called Ráŕh. The area north of the Padma was called Barind in Bengali. In Sanskrit the word was further refined to “Barendra”. And the area east of the Padma was called Vauṋga, comprising Mymensingh, Dhaka, Faridpur, Barishal. And still further east was known as Cat́t́al or Shriibhúmi – now Sylhet or Shriihat́t́a. These five districts constituted Bengal.
summary: In olden days southern Bengal was known as Samatat.
In Sanskrit the word was further refined to “Barendra”.
These five districts constituted Bengal.

paragraphs.text: King Shalibahan was the king of this Samatat. He said that the lunar system would not suit Bengal. These days the Farsi word sál is used [to mean “year”]; the adjective form is sáláná (Farsi), but that is originally a Bengali term. Shalibahan introduced the system of solar year. That is why a year is called shál, after his name. Shál means “solar year”. The calculations of the solar year were performed in ancient India according to the [Súryasiddhánta-reckoner].(8) A reckoner is called sárańii in Bengali. Such a sárańii led to the [Indian system until the late 1950ʼs] of the t́áká [rupee], the áná [1/16 of a rupee] and the pái [1/192 of a rupee]. The astrologers started using the sárańii to get the degree of angular position of the sun, etc. (they themselves did not do the detailed calculations). The Súryasiddhánta-Sárańii [sárańii based on the Súryasiddhánta] was used then and is still used today.
summary: King Shalibahan was the king of this Samatat.
The calculations of the solar year were performed in ancient India according to the [Súryasiddhánta-reckoner].
The Súryasiddhánta-Sárańii [sárańii based on the Súryasiddhánta] was used then and is still used today.

paragraphs.text: The sun changes its course, and the stars and planets also change their courses. The solar and lunar calendars change accordingly. Based on the changes in the courses of the stars and planets, other calendars can also be prepared, which can be called sidereal calendars or sidereal years or sidereal paiṋjikás [almanacs]. But these are also changing. So can we stick [for example] to the Súryasiddhánta-Sárańii these days? Suppose it is indicated in the almanac, that is, the Súryasiddhánta-Sárańii , that a lunar eclipse will take place at 6:30. Now, if you follow the almanac you will not see the lunar eclipse, for the eclipse will take place one hundred minutes later. The almanac fails. So the calendar based on that almanac is now incorrect, and calculations based on that calendar today are also incorrect.
summary: The sun changes its course, and the stars and planets also change their courses.
So can we stick [for example] to the Súryasiddhánta-Sárańii these days?
So the calendar based on that almanac is now incorrect, and calculations based on that calendar today are also incorrect.

paragraphs.text: If [amid all the wrong calculations] astrologers wrongly predict an eclipse time in this way, people will easily catch them. For example, it may say in the almanac that an eclipse will take place at 6:40 p.m., but it actually takes place at 7:40; then people blame the astrologers. To avoid that situation, astrologers consult the marine almanacs to get the exact times of the ebb tide and the flow tide. This is their own system of calculation! Accordingly, they write [in their sárańiis] that the eclipse will start at a particular time. All the other calculations [in their sárańiis] are defective.
summary: If [amid all the wrong calculations] astrologers wrongly predict an eclipse time in this way, people will easily catch them.
To avoid that situation, astrologers consult the marine almanacs to get the exact times of the ebb tide and the flow tide.
All the other calculations [in their sárańiis] are defective.

paragraphs.text: About six hundred years ago, a great scholar was born at Vikrampur, who with much effort prepared a new reckoner. He was very young – about twenty or twenty-three years old – but he was very intelligent and active. He showed his new reckoner to the scholars of Nabadwip. It gave the exact calculations, avoiding all mistakes. The Brahmin scholars of Nabadwip grew extremely jealous of him. That evening at 7:00, an eclipse was to take place; but according to that young man the eclipse would be seen at 7:30. He challenged the Nabadwip astrologers, “Look, just watch when the eclipse really takes place. Then you may either accept or reject my observation.” That night at 7:00 sharp, the young man took a jug of water(9) and squatted down to urinate. The elderly scholars objected. saying, “What a sacrilege! You dare to take a jug of water and urinate at the time of an eclipse!”
summary: About six hundred years ago, a great scholar was born at Vikrampur, who with much effort prepared a new reckoner.
He challenged the Nabadwip astrologers, “Look, just watch when the eclipse really takes place.
You dare to take a jug of water and urinate at the time of an eclipse!

paragraphs.text: The young man replied, “No, no, I am not doing as you say.” Then he said, “Ámi Nader mate muti.” This latter utterance may be interpreted in two ways: 1) “I am urinating [at the eclipse time] according to the Nadia system of calculation;”(10) 2) “The Nadia system of calculation is so defective that I am urinating on that system.” According to some people, the young astrologer was murdered. If that brilliant man had been allowed to survive, he could have introduced remarkable changes in the system of astrological calculation.
summary: The young man replied, “No, no, I am not doing as you say.

” This latter utterance may be interpreted in two ways: 1) “I am urinating [at the eclipse time] according to the Nadia system of calculation;”(10) 2) “The Nadia system of calculation is so defective that I am urinating on that system.
If that brilliant man had been allowed to survive, he could have introduced remarkable changes in the system of astrological calculation.

paragraphs.text: Another great scholar, Jayanta Panigrahii, was born in the Contai (Kanthi) area in Midnapur. By his great efforts, he also introduced a new reckoner. His views on astrological calculation remain true even today. However, since many more changes have since occurred, the present reckoner should also be revised. Perhaps you know that the same Bengalee calendar is prevalent over a vast area – Assam, Manipur, Tripura, Bangladesh, West Bengal, Orissa, Chotanagpur, Santhal Pargana and Purnia.
summary: Another great scholar, Jayanta Panigrahii, was born in the Contai (Kanthi) area in Midnapur.
His views on astrological calculation remain true even today.
Perhaps you know that the same Bengalee calendar is prevalent over a vast area – Assam, Manipur, Tripura, Bangladesh, West Bengal, Orissa, Chotanagpur, Santhal Pargana and Purnia.

paragraphs.text: In Orissa, another great scholar was born, whose name was [Chandra Shekhar] Samanta. He prepared a new almanac, taking great pains. Generally speaking, that almanac is still popular, but it too has to be revised. The astrologers of the Siddhánta Paiṋjiká are trying to submit a correct calculation. I cannot say which one is perfect; but surely we will have to calculate accurately.
summary: In Orissa, another great scholar was born, whose name was [Chandra Shekhar] Samanta.
Generally speaking, that almanac is still popular, but it too has to be revised.
I cannot say which one is perfect; but surely we will have to calculate accurately.

paragraphs.text: Thus in the path of movement through various changes, we now enter the [Bengalee] year 1386. The sun enters the zodiac sign Aries. As long as the sun is in Aries, the month of Vaeshákh will last. Thus time moves on; it knows no end.
summary: Thus in the path of movement through various changes, we now enter the [Bengalee] year 1386.
As long as the sun is in Aries, the month of Vaeshákh will last.
Thus time moves on; it knows no end.

paragraphs.text: I have given you a brief history of the Bengalee race. The scholars who used to do astrological calculations in Bengal were called Ácárya Brahmins. They had a powerful centre in Bali. Prior to that, they used to live in Kolkata. But following the execution of Maharaj Nandakumar [by the British], the reputed Brahmins deserted Kolkata, thinking that an extremely heinous act – the killing of a Brahmin – had been committed on the soil of Kolkata. Most of them settled in Bali, for Kolkata was then considered an unholy land. The pandits of Bali do calculations even today as do the Nabadwip and Bhatpara [North 24 Parganas] scholars.
summary: I have given you a brief history of the Bengalee race.
Prior to that, they used to live in Kolkata.
The pandits of Bali do calculations even today as do the Nabadwip and Bhatpara [North 24 Parganas] scholars.

paragraphs.text: Thus I have given you at least a brief summary of Bengalʼs history.
summary: Thus I have given you at least a brief summary of Bengalʼs history.

paragraphs.text: Not in the Ráŕh of black soil, but in the Ráŕh of laterite (red) soil, lie the following villages: Bandyogháti of Birbhum district (the original abode of the Bandyopádhyáyas, or Banerjees); Mukhot́i village of Bankura district (the original abode of the Mukhopádhyáyas, or Mukherjees); Chát́uti of West Burdwan (the ancestral home of the Chat́t́opádhyáyas, or Chatterjees); Ghośli of Manbhum (the ancestral home of the Ghośáls); and Gauṋgolii of West Burdwan District (the ancestral home of the Gauṋgopádhyáyas or Gauṋguliis). All these villages are located in the land of laterite soil; none is in the area of black soil. The Baul school of music also originated in the area of laterite soil. In the study of history, this significant fact should be remembered.

paragraphs.text: So this land of Ráŕh is composed of laterite soil. The eastern part of Ráŕh is composed of black soil, because that part has been formed from alluvial soil carried by the rivers. It is not exactly red because pacá gáchpála [humus or decomposed vegetation] is also mixed with the red soil. Thus the eastern Burdwan, Howrah and Hooghly Districts are very fertile. The remaining portion of Ráŕh, which is composed of laterite soil, is gradually eroding.
summary: So this land of Ráŕh is composed of laterite soil.
It is not exactly red because pacá gáchpála [humus or decomposed vegetation] is also mixed with the red soil.
The remaining portion of Ráŕh, which is composed of laterite soil, is gradually eroding.

paragraphs.text: But how was this laterite soil formed? It has come from the constant erosion of the hills. The small hills which we see today were medium-sized hills in the past, and the undulating highlands of red soil were once great hills. Now those hills have been reduced to mere anthills. And where the land is still very high, we must infer that these were once extremely lofty peaks which in the gradual process of erosion have been reduced to small mounds. The land of Ráŕh flows in waves of hills and valleys: where the crests are lower, these areas were once valleys and smaller hills; and where the land is comparatively high, there the hills were extremely lofty. All of these hills have undergone, and are still undergoing, a gradual process of erosion. If someone travels past Bolepur station by train, one will invariably come across huge areas of extreme soil erosion (khoyái in Ráŕhii Bengali): it seems as if the skeletons of the hills are exposed. And when that soil gradually flows down towards the sea, it creates new fertile lands. By large-scale afforestation, this type of extreme erosion can be checked – there is no other alternative. In fact, it is extremely necessary now to create large new forests by afforestation, so the roots of the trees will hold the soil and prevent erosion. Of course, it is not true that the entire red soil has been lost.
summary: But how was this laterite soil formed?
All of these hills have undergone, and are still undergoing, a gradual process of erosion.
Of course, it is not true that the entire red soil has been lost.

paragraphs.text: Previously this whole area was completely hilly; in fact Birbhum, West Burdwan and Bankura were all hills. Thus we find this vast area of undulating land today. If there is a slight increase of rainfall, tea cultivation will be very successful. In fact, tea plantation requires just this type of land. Even coffee and cocoa may be cultivated there, because the land is sloping.

paragraphs.text: Along these high slopes one may discover many heavy minerals. In the ancient past this was a belt of hard rock; it was neither an area of sedimentary rock created by volcanic eruption, nor igneous rock; rather it was metamorphic rock (formed by extreme pressure under the ground). Wherever the land is undulating in Bankura, Birbhum, West Burdwan, Purulia etc., one can discover heavy minerals buried deep within the earth. Actually these are being discovered even now: there is a strong likelihood that great deposits of gold and copper will be found there. If the people of Bengal prepare a detailed plan for the future, they will have to take these possibilities into consideration, and accordingly they can develop industries in the area. But this will not be easy; it will demand hard labour. As Swami Vivekananda once said, nothing is accomplished without toil.

paragraphs.text: Kalá [systaltic flow] gets transformed into káśt́há [linear flow] as a result of pulsating movement through crest and trough. What happens then? At specific points in time, one begins to gain control over particular thoughts. It is noticed that sometimes one has control over a particular thought but may not have such control at another point in time. Sometimes one has control over a certain thought, and at other times over some other thought. Sometimes one has control over anger but no control over greed. It may so happen that one does not have a weakness for wealth, name and fame but has no control over oneself while taking food. There was a chief minister who was well known to me. He was a good person who never used to accept bribes. He was good in all respects, but when he was given flattened rice (cuŕá), curd and sweet cake (peŕá), he would pay no heed to how much he had eaten. And so it goes.
summary: Kalá [systaltic flow] gets transformed into káśt́há [linear flow] as a result of pulsating movement through crest and trough.
Sometimes one has control over anger but no control over greed.
He was good in all respects, but when he was given flattened rice (cuŕá), curd and sweet cake (peŕá), he would pay no heed to how much he had eaten.

paragraphs.text: In one matter we have no greed, but in another we have tremendous greed. These all belong to the category of vyatireka. It is called vyatireka because when kalá is getting transformed into káśt́há (it is not always the case that kalá shall be transformed into káśt́há), sometimes káśt́há becomes smaller than the kalá, while at other times, under the pressure of káśt́há, the subsequent kalá becomes larger than its normal state. That is why the state of vyatireka is very perplexing. For example, some women may have no greed whatsoever for food but strong weakness for saŕis. That is also a kind of greed. In certain cases, one has control and in other cases one is unable to maintain that control. Someone insults her in an abusive manner, and she endures it all quietly. People will say that she endures like mother earth. But she flies into a rage if anyone criticizes members of her fatherʼs family. Sometimes she has full control and at other times she has no control at all. People are like this. This stage is known as the state of vyatireka. In this state one must remain vigilant so that one might be able to exercise this control in all situations.
summary: In one matter we have no greed, but in another we have tremendous greed.
Someone insults her in an abusive manner, and she endures it all quietly.
In this state one must remain vigilant so that one might be able to exercise this control in all situations.

paragraphs.text: In the stage of vyatireka the obstacles appear more from within than from without. These obstacles are psychic in nature. For example, when in the course of sádhaná one attains the state of yatamána, then obstacles appear from all sides. Family members create obstructions. The environ-ment creates obstructions. But in the stage of vyatireka there is hardly any external obstruction. The disorder is internal. In one matter one gains control and in another one does not. There are some people who perhaps do not get angry, no matter what. So-and-so is a very good and innocent person but he becomes irritated when he sees specific individuals. It may be that a man is dreaded like the god death by his subordinates in the office because of his stern personality but at home he gets broom lashings from his wife. There he endures it. That means that his characteristic sternness is not always present. You will find many such persons in the world. You laugh when you hear me say this, but it is a significant aspect of human psychology. Do you understand? You have to exercise control at this stage.
summary: In the stage of vyatireka the obstacles appear more from within than from without.
In one matter one gains control and in another one does not.
You have to exercise control at this stage.

paragraphs.text: Consider the matter of food. A certain person has no greed in all other matters but he is crazy for roasted brinjal. What an ordinary thing it is, roasted brinjal, you see, but he is under its sway. This type of psychology is very delicate. One has to deal cautiously with such issues. While dealing with such a person if we wrongly think – “He is a great man, should he be so crazy for roasted brinjal?” – then we are grossly mistaken. Rather we should give that great man puffed rice with roasted brinjal. Then only you can influence him.
summary: Consider the matter of food.
One has to deal cautiously with such issues.
Then only you can influence him.

paragraphs.text: Now in the state of vyatireka, it is easy to discover what type of weakness a person has. If you study behavioural psychology then when you see this state of vyatireka you will be able to understand where an indivi-dualʼs weakness lies. Evil-minded persons can accomplish many things by taking advantage of a personʼs weakness. This is how cunning people serve their interests, by taking advantage of that personʼs foolishness. You should remain vigilant that when you are in such a state of vyatireka you should be conscious of your weaknesses, so that others do not become aware of them. You may have the opportunity to know the weaknesses of others, but you should not let others have the same opportunity.
summary: Now in the state of vyatireka, it is easy to discover what type of weakness a person has.
This is how cunning people serve their interests, by taking advantage of that personʼs foolishness.
You may have the opportunity to know the weaknesses of others, but you should not let others have the same opportunity.

paragraphs.text: You know about the cultural diversities among the Aryans and the non-Aryans. In the land of the non-Aryans, the instrument by which paddy and other such grains are threshed is called dheṋki in Bengali. According to the system of Aryan civilization, that which is used for threshing is called udukhala.(1) In Hindi, it is kupri. There is no Sanskrit equivalent of dheṋki. Dheṋki is an indigenous expression.
summary: You know about the cultural diversities among the Aryans and the non-Aryans.
In Hindi, it is kupri.
Dheṋki is an indigenous expression.

paragraphs.text: So the Aryans used the term udukhala. One has to strain oneself more while using the udukhala. One has to exert the strength of the hand for threshing. This is not done while using the dheṋki, only the leg is used. In udukhala, one has to thresh using the hands. Particles jump up while the dheṋki is used; so is the case with the udukhala. The rice granules bounce about, and in the course of this jumping, rice is prepared. Rice cannot come out of the paddy without this jumping. So, that whose nature is to jump is called tańd́ula in Sanskrit. Tańd́u + la + da become tańd́ula. The Bengali equivalent of tańd́ula is cául. In contemporary Bengali, it is cál. Cául used to be sold [in the market] during the period of the Mauṋgalkávya.(2)
summary: So the Aryans used the term udukhala.
The rice granules bounce about, and in the course of this jumping, rice is prepared.

paragraphs.text: The Bengali word [for dhán, uncooked rice] is cául. How is cául derived? As “that which has been cálá [winnowed] by a súrpa or kulo [a winnowing basket].” How is it winnowed? First the chaff is separated out, then the khud [small fragments], then the husk; then only does one get cául or cál [uncooked rice]. The word khud is derived from the Sanskrit word kśudra. So, that which is left after being sifted is called cául. In old Bengali it is cául. Anything which has been winnowed [cálá] is called cául. It may not necessarily be rice grains.
summary: The Bengali word [for dhán, uncooked rice] is cául.
The word khud is derived from the Sanskrit word kśudra.
It may not necessarily be rice grains.

paragraphs.text: Táńd́ava is that which is related to jumping (lamphan). Táńd́ava involves ullamphan. What is the difference between lamphan and ullamphan? Lamphan involves jumping while remaining connected with the earth. One can jump while standing and touching the earth. However, when jumping high, there must be separation from the earth. This is called ́ullamphanʼ (ut-lamphan = ullamphan). So what is the táńd́ava dance? Is it ullamphan or lamphan? It is ullamphan.
summary: Táńd́ava is that which is related to jumping (lamphan).
One can jump while standing and touching the earth.
Is it ullamphan or lamphan?

paragraphs.text: Sadáshiva introduced the táńd́ava dance. Why did He do that? How did He do it? There are many lymphatic glands and endocrine glands in our body. Hormones secreted from these glands permeate the entire body. The hormones secreted through táńd́ava generate greater manliness and courage in the person. That is why hormones are secreted from the lymphatic glands and greater manliness is produced in those who practise táńd́ava.
summary: Sadáshiva introduced the táńd́ava dance.
Hormones secreted from these glands permeate the entire body.
That is why hormones are secreted from the lymphatic glands and greater manliness is produced in those who practise táńd́ava.

paragraphs.text: Since the practice of táńd́ava stimulates manliness, it is prohibited for women. What are other results that follow? The pineal gland (sahasrára cakra) and pituitary gland (ájiṋácakra) are activated. As a result of this, the memory is enhanced and the brain is strengthened. Cells in the brain are also strengthened. There is no specific exercise for the brain. Táńd́ava is the only exercise for the brain. So considering all these, táńd́ava dance was introduced.
summary: Since the practice of táńd́ava stimulates manliness, it is prohibited for women.
Cells in the brain are also strengthened.
So considering all these, táńd́ava dance was introduced.

paragraphs.text: But what do the dancers carry in their hands? Completeness in human life is brought about through struggles and clashes. One who loves struggle, will have to wade through struggles, and one who does not like it, will also have to pass through struggle. One cannot afford to avoid struggle. If someone says, “I do not want to struggle,” it is an impossibility. What shall such a person do when one is hit by a hammer? Then, they will go to those who love struggle and say, “Save me, brother, save me.” Is it not better that while bearing the blows, one prepares oneself to counter the challenges ahead?
summary: But what do the dancers carry in their hands?
If someone says, “I do not want to struggle,” it is an impossibility.
” Is it not better that while bearing the blows, one prepares oneself to counter the challenges ahead?

paragraphs.text: If a person has the potential to give a strong counter-blow, what is the point in shying away from encounters? Now, what is the significance of objects which the dancers carry in their hands while doing táńd́ava? They signify, “I am moving ahead, wading through clashes and counter-clashes.” Force can be applied for the collective welfare as and when it is necessary.
summary: If a person has the potential to give a strong counter-blow, what is the point in shying away from encounters?
They signify, “I am moving ahead, wading through clashes and counter-clashes.
” Force can be applied for the collective welfare as and when it is necessary.

paragraphs.text: There are three pathways in Tantra – dakśiń márga [rightward path], váma márga [leftward path] and madhyama márga [middle path]. In Buddhist philosophy there is neither right nor left path. There is only the middle path (madhyamá márga or madhyam márga). What are the things that find a place in the dancerʼs hands? The dancer, may, for instance, hold a human skull in the left hand and a dagger in the right hand. Or in the daytime one may, if one wishes, hold a snake in the left hand. [At night] one may hold a d́ambaru [a small drum shaped like an hourglass] or a mashál [torch] in the right hand.(3) One can recognize everything by the light of a torch and can understand by the sound of a drum. Otherwise at night, neither a skull nor a snake can be recognized. In the left hand, there is the symbol of destruction and death.
summary: There are three pathways in Tantra – dakśiń márga [rightward path], váma márga [leftward path] and madhyama márga [middle path].
Or in the daytime one may, if one wishes, hold a snake in the left hand.
In the left hand, there is the symbol of destruction and death.

paragraphs.text: How does the individual move ahead? There is Hari on one side and Hara on the other. On the one side there is progress; on the other side there is destruction. While Hara symbolizes destruction, Hari symbolizes creation. The world moves on through the clash of Hari and Hara (Hariharátmaka). A small and beautiful bud appears on a plant.The flower blooms, unfolds itself completely. Till now, there is the sport of Hari. Thereafter the play of Hara begins. The petals wither and fall off, one after the other. As there is creation on the one hand, destruction awaits on the other. Sometimes we die and sometimes we live. The individual has to move ahead through struggles. One has nothing to fear. Why should one fear death? People have to attain immortality by waging war against death. This is our sádhaná. Humanity is moving ahead with great speed, with the vigour and power of the Supreme Entity. Why should one yield to any obstruction? Nothing should awaken fear. Even if fear stares one in the face, one must not fear. Having been defeated, the fear will rapidly recede. The God of struggle, Sadáshiva, is the death of death. That is to say, He is as dreadful as death, for death itself.
summary: How does the individual move ahead?
The individual has to move ahead through struggles.
That is to say, He is as dreadful as death, for death itself.

paragraphs.text: So the individual has to keep on fighting. A person must continue to fight without any respite. The dagger is the functional symbol of struggle. So wage a vigorous struggle against obstacles that have come or shall come on the path of progress. And what should one have as oneʼs garment? The tiger skin or a red garment. The tiger skin (vyághracarma) in actuality means mrgacarma [forest-animal skin]. In Sanskrit, mrga means animals that live in the forest. Many think that mrga means only deer. But this is not so. All those animals that live in the forest are called mrga. Monkeys are called shákhámrga because they live on the shákhá [branches] of trees. In olden days kings used to visit the forest for hunting (mrgayá), but not only to hunt the deer. So the animal skin or the red garment means, “I am using it as my cloth by annihilating the brute force.” A red garment means that I am sitting on the mutative force and I am using the mutative quality as my outer clothing. The red colour is indicative of the mutative quality.(4)
summary: So the individual has to keep on fighting.
In Sanskrit, mrga means animals that live in the forest.
The red colour is indicative of the mutative quality.
